name: The Fool
symbols: A youth steps toward a cliff edge, face lifted to the sky rather than the drop — the beginning made without calculating the fall.
A small white dog at his heels barks — instinct, the animal self that both warns and accompanies.
In one hand a white rose (purity of motive); over the shoulder a small bundle on a staff (the light baggage of one who travels unencumbered).
The sun rises behind him and mountains lie ahead — the known at his back, the unknown before him.

reading.upright: The Fool is the beginning that precedes knowledge: stepping into the unknown with openness rather than certainty. It favours first steps, spontaneity, and trust in one's own footing — the fall is real, but so is the ground.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Fool loses his balance: either the leap becomes heedless, taken without looking, or the edge becomes paralyzing and the step is never taken. It asks which of the two fears is at work.

name: The Magician
symbols: A figure raises a wand to the sky while pointing to the earth — will above, matter below, the channel between them made active.
The infinity symbol above his head — limitlessness of the potential being concentrated into a single act.
A table before him holds a cup, sword, coin and wand — all four elements of the world, gathered and available.
Roses and lilies in the garden behind him — desire and thought in bloom, the raw material of his work.

reading.upright: The Magician is the moment of concentrated will — everything needed is already on the table, and the task is to focus it. Skill, initiative, and the deliberate use of one's resources.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Magician's power is misused or dispersed: tricks instead of craft, manipulation instead of direction, or talent left on the table unused.

name: The High Priestess
symbols: She sits between a black pillar and a white one — the two poles of experience, held in balance rather than resolved.
A crescent moon at her feet — the subconscious, the tide, the reflected light of what is not yet known.
Behind her a veil of pomegranates — the fruit of Persephone, marking the threshold to the underworld of the hidden.
A scroll marked TORA rests half-hidden in her lap — esoteric law, given only to those who look.

reading.upright: The High Priestess is the knowledge that arrives before explanation — intuition, dreams, the quiet sense of what is true. She asks for stillness and attention rather than action.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Priestess is either secreting what should be shared, or the querent is ignoring the inner voice in favour of the surface story.

name: The Empress
symbols: She reclines on cushions in an open field — ease, sensuality, the body at rest in the world.
A field of ripe wheat lies before her — harvest, fertility, the reward of nature's slow work.
A crown of twelve stars — cosmic order, the whole zodiac gathered on a single head.
A heart-shaped shield marked with the sign of Venus — love and creativity as her domain.

reading.upright: The Empress is abundance that arrives through the body and the natural world: fertility, generosity, beauty, and the slow ripening of what has been tended.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Empress's abundance is blocked or distorted — creativity stalled, nurture turned into smothering, or self-neglect mistaken for modesty.

name: The Emperor
symbols: He sits on a stone throne carved with rams' heads — Aries, the sign of initiative, marking authority that has been earned.
He holds an ankh scepter in one hand and a globe in the other — life and dominion, held together.
Armor shows beneath his red robe — power that is ready, even when at rest.
Bare mountains rise behind him — the stark, unyielding ground on which order is built.

reading.upright: The Emperor is structure, law, and the protective authority that makes a life possible. He represents the father-principle: boundaries, responsibility, and the decision to take charge.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Emperor becomes domination, rigidity, or the absence of a spine — either too much control or none at all.

name: The Hierophant
symbols: He raises his right hand in blessing — the gesture of the one authorised to transmit.
A triple crown marks the three worlds of body, mind and spirit — hierarchy spanning all of them.
Two crossed keys lie at his feet — the keys to sacred knowledge, kept by the institution.
Two tonsured monks kneel before him — the faithful receiving the transmitted teaching.

reading.upright: The Hierophant is the institution and the inherited form: tradition, education, the shared belief that holds a community together. He asks what has been handed down.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Hierophant asks whether the inherited form still serves — a call to rebel against dogma, or to find one's own spiritual authority.

name: The Lovers
symbols: A man and a woman stand beneath a winged angel — the human pair under the blessing of a larger unity.
Behind the woman, a tree with fruit — appetite, temptation, the knowledge of good and evil.
Behind the man, a tree with flames — passion, desire, the fire of the will.
A mountain rises between them — the obstacle or choice that the union must pass through.

reading.upright: The Lovers is union — of two people, of two parts of the self, or of one's actions with one's values. It is also the choice that such union requires.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Lovers point to misalignment: a relationship or a decision that does not match the deeper self, or avoidance of the choice.

name: The Chariot
symbols: An armored figure drives a chariot — force directed by a will that stays at the reins.
Two sphinxes, one black and one white, pull the chariot — opposing forces, reconciled by the driver's hand.
A starry canopy hangs above — the cosmic support of a well-aimed action.
A walled city recedes behind him — the safety he has left in order to move.

reading.upright: The Chariot is directed will — the capacity to hold opposing forces together long enough to move. Victory through discipline, momentum, and clear aim.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Chariot's force scatters: no clear destination, the reins dropped, or aggression mistaken for direction.

name: Strength
symbols: A woman calmly opens (or closes) a lion's jaws — not force, but the gentle mastery of a wild thing.
The infinity symbol hovers above her head — limitless patience, an inner resource without end.
She is dressed in white — purity of intention, the calm that gentleness requires.
The lion itself is the passion she handles — not killed, but befriended.

reading.upright: Strength is inner power, not force: the courage to meet one's own wildness with patience, to master by gentleness. It favours softness over struggle.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the lion is running the show — self-doubt, raw impulse, or the fear that gentleness is weakness.

name: The Hermit
symbols: An old man stands alone on a snowy peak — elevation, the long climb toward understanding.
He holds a lantern in which a single star burns — his own inner light, carried into the dark.
A staff supports him — the simple, unglamorous support that makes the journey possible.
His back is turned to us — the inward direction of his attention.

reading.upright: The Hermit is deliberate solitude — the withdrawal that lets one hear oneself. Wisdom earned by looking inward, and the willingness to walk alone for a time.
reading.reversed: Reversed, solitude has become isolation: the withdrawal that no longer returns, or a loneliness that hides rather than seeks.

name: Wheel of Fortune
symbols: A great wheel turns in the sky — the law of return, the cycle no one escapes.
A sphinx sits atop the wheel with a sword — the riddle, and the balance the wheel demands.
A serpent descends on one side while Anubis rises on the other — descent and ascent, the twin motions of fortune.
Four winged creatures hold the corners — the four elements, the fixed points that the turning wheel requires.

reading.upright: The Wheel of Fortune is the turning of cycles — the recognition that fate, luck and time move in patterns larger than the will. A turning point.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the wheel is resisted or repeating: bad luck, or the same pattern returning because it has not been understood.

name: Justice
symbols: She holds a sword perfectly upright — reason, cutting cleanly through what is unclear.
In her other hand, scales — the careful weighing of what cannot be decided by force.
She wears a crown — truth has authority here.
A red robe falls from her shoulders — the active, living quality of real judgment.

reading.upright: Justice is the principle of consequence: what is true, what is fair, and what follows from what. It asks for honest accounting and clear sight.
reading.reversed: Reversed, Justice is miscarried: dishonesty, imbalance, or the refusal to face a consequence. It asks where the scale is being hidden.

name: The Hanged Man
symbols: A figure hangs upside down from a living tree — a reversal that is chosen, not suffered.
A halo glows around his head — illumination arriving through the inversion.
His legs form a triangle — stability within the suspension.
His face is calm — the absence of struggle that makes the reversal possible.

reading.upright: The Hanged Man is willing suspension: stopping, hanging between, and letting a new perspective arrive. Sacrifice that is chosen rather than imposed.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Hanged Man has become a stalling: an avoidance disguised as patience, or a sacrifice that has curdled into martyrdom.

name: Death
symbols: A skeleton rides a white horse — the inescapable change, coming regardless of rank or preparation.
He carries a black banner with a white rose — the end, marked by purity rather than horror.
A king lies fallen beneath the horse — no position survives the change.
Between two towers the sun rises — a new dawn that can only appear once the old has passed.

reading.upright: Death is transformation, not literal death: the ending that makes the next form possible. Release, change, and the clearing away of what has finished.
reading.reversed: Reversed, Death is resisted: change refused, a stage clung to after it has ended, and the resulting stagnation.

name: Temperance
symbols: An angel pours water between two cups — the careful mixing of elements into something new.
One foot stands in a pool, the other on land — the conscious and unconscious held together.
A path winds toward the sun — the long, patient route of the work.
Irises grow beside her — faith, and the flower of the rainbow that follows the storm.

reading.upright: Temperance is the alchemy of balance: patience, the blending of opposites, and the slow work of making one thing out of two. Moderation and faithful process.
reading.reversed: Reversed, Temperance has tipped: excess, haste, or an incompatible mixing that cannot hold.

name: The Devil
symbols: A horned, bat-winged figure presides — the shadow, the part of the self that binds.
Two figures are chained to his pedestal — but the chains hang loose around their necks.
An inverted pentagram above his head — spirit turned upside down, matter at the top.
A torch is held downward — the fire of the will misused, burning toward the ground.

reading.upright: The Devil is bondage — but bondage that is largely chosen. Materialism, addiction, a shadow that has been given more power than it has.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Devil is seen for what he is: the chains are recognised, and the work of release begins.

name: The Tower
symbols: Lightning strikes the crown from the top of a tower — the false certainty that has been built up is not the truth.
Two figures fall headfirst — the fall is unavoidable, and it is total.
The tower stands on a jagged peak — the structure was already precarious, and everyone knew.
Flames pour from the windows — the destruction is also a revelation; the tower was never what it claimed.

reading.upright: The Tower is sudden, total disruption: a structure built on false certainty is torn down. Not punishment but revelation — the truth breaking through what could no longer stand.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Tower is delayed or resisted: a disaster held off, or an inner upheaval that has not yet broken the surface.

name: The Star
symbols: A nude figure pours water onto the land and into a pool — unselfconscious giving, in both directions.
One foot rests in the pool, the other on land — the two worlds, kept together.
Eight stars shine above — regeneration, the number of return after the storm.
An ibis on a nearby tree — wisdom, watching from its own place.

reading.upright: The Star is the calm after the Tower: hope, healing, and the quiet return of inspiration. It favours faith in the process and trust in what is being rebuilt.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Star is dimmed: hope lost, faith in the process exhausted, and a tiredness that cannot yet see renewal.

name: The Moon
symbols: A moon with a face shines in a deep sky — light that reflects rather than reveals, casting the world in doubt.
A dog and a wolf howl at it — the tame and the wild instinct, both made uneasy by the night.
A crayfish crawls out of a pool — the deep, unrecognised material rising to the surface.
A path leads between two towers — the way forward is narrow, and only partly visible.

reading.upright: The Moon is ambiguity and illusion: what is seen is not clearly what is there. It favours intuition over certainty, and patience while the unclear clarifies.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Moon's fog is lifting — a confusion begins to resolve, a hidden thing comes into view.

name: The Sun
symbols: A child rides a white horse — innocent confidence, fully at ease in the light.
Sunflowers turn openly toward the sun — growth that is not ashamed of its own wanting.
A red banner flies behind the child — the vital energy of a life that is being lived.
A walled garden surrounds him — safety, but a safety with open sky above it.

reading.upright: The Sun is the uncomplicated good: joy, clarity, vitality, and the sense that things are, on the whole, going well. Success that can be felt as well as known.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Sun is behind a cloud: joy available but not quite reached, pessimism colouring what is actually fine.

name: Judgement
symbols: An angel blows a trumpet — the call that cannot be unheard, arriving from beyond the self.
Figures rise from coffins with arms lifted — resurrection, the answering of the call.
A banner bears a cross — the union of above and below, spirit entering the world.
Mountains recede behind — the past, present but no longer in front.

reading.upright: Judgement is the awakening: the call that summons one to account and to rise. Reckoning, forgiveness, and the willingness to answer what has been heard.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the call is refused — self-doubt, harsh judgment of the self, or the coffin lid kept closed.

name: The World
symbols: A figure stands inside a great wreath — the whole cycle, embraced rather than escaped.
Two wands are held in her hands — will and matter, finally balanced.
Four creatures hold the corners — the four elements, now in their places.
A scarf or veil moves around her — the completion is alive, still in motion.

reading.upright: The World is the completion of a cycle: wholeness, fulfilment, and the arrival at a place from which the next beginning can be seen.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the World is near-completion: the last step delayed, or the cycle finished in form but not yet in meaning.

name: Ace of Wands
symbols: A hand emerges from a cloud holding a living wand — the gift arrives from beyond the self.
Leaves sprout from the wand — the potential is alive, still growing.
A castle stands on a distant hill — the goal the spark is aimed at.
Sparks of light fall from the wand — the raw energy of an idea before it has been shaped.

reading.upright: The Ace of Wands is the spark: raw inspiration, a new venture, the moment before form. It favours the first yes, and the courage to begin.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the spark is delayed or refused: a start that has not quite caught, a false start, or the idea held too long.

name: Two of Wands
symbols: A figure holds a globe — the whole world, considered from a height.
Two wands mark a boundary — the moment of choosing a direction.
A castle stands on a hill — the home that is being weighed against the wider world.
Sea and horizon open behind — the unknown that is being contemplated.

reading.upright: The Two of Wands is the planning that follows the spark: weighing where to go, what to take on, whether to leave. Ambition, seen clearly.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Two of Wands hesitates: the decision postponed, the vision narrowed to what is already safe.

name: Three of Wands
symbols: A figure stands on a height looking out — the vantage of those who have already begun.
Three wands are planted — the plan is now established.
Ships sail toward the horizon — goods, news, or opportunity travelling.
The far horizon is open — the future is larger than the present.

reading.upright: The Three of Wands is progress: the plan is in motion, and one's reach extends beyond the immediate. Foresight, expansion, and the patience to wait for return.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Three of Wands stalls: the expansion is frustrated, the horizon looks closed, or the plan is too small.

name: Four of Wands
symbols: Four wands form a canopy of flowers — the home, celebrated and open.
Two figures raise bouquets — community, the shared joy.
A castle stands behind — the home that has been made.
A bridge or path is visible below — the way in, open to guests.

reading.upright: The Four of Wands is homecoming and celebration: the harvest gathered, the household made, the community rejoicing together.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Four of Wands is unsettled: domestic instability, an unwelcome arrival, or a milestone that cannot yet be celebrated.

name: Five of Wands
symbols: Five figures spar with wands — competition, the jostling of many claims.
The stances are disorderly — no clear form to the conflict.
No one is clearly winning — the struggle is ongoing, not concluded.
The sky is bright — the conflict has an energy, not a despair.

reading.upright: The Five of Wands is friction: competing claims, disagreement, the energy of a contest. Often it is sparring rather than war.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the conflict is avoided or internalised: the fight that will not be had, or the fight that has become a private one.

name: Six of Wands
symbols: A rider on a white horse holds a wand crowned with a wreath — triumph, publicly carried.
A crowd surrounds him — recognition, the shared acknowledgment.
A laurel on his head — honour, earned and displayed.
A green cloak — the vitality of a victory that is still fresh.

reading.upright: The Six of Wands is recognition: the win that is seen, the success that is acknowledged. Confidence, momentum, and the reward of having been right.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the victory is not acknowledged — either it has not been seen, or the pride has gone before the fall.

name: Seven of Wands
symbols: A figure stands on high ground, holding one wand against six — disadvantage held from a position of advantage.
Six wands press in from below — the opposition is real and coordinated.
The figure is not falling — the stance is holding.
Uneven ground — the contested terrain matters.

reading.upright: The Seven of Wands is standing one's ground: defense of what has been built, perseverance against pressure, the willingness to be contested.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the defense is failing: overwhelm, compromise, or the decision that this is not the fight to have.

name: Eight of Wands
symbols: Eight wands fly through the air, none touching the ground — motion, release, speed.
There are no figures — the events themselves are the subject.
A river or landscape below — the destination is real, just not yet reached.
Even spacing — the motion is ordered, not chaotic.

reading.upright: The Eight of Wands is speed: news arriving, things moving fast, the sudden acceleration of what had been waiting.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Eight of Wands is delayed: movement halted, news that does not arrive, the slowdown that frustrates.

name: Nine of Wands
symbols: A figure leans on a wand, bandaged — the wounds already taken, the strength still standing.
Eight wands stand behind him like a fence — the barrier is real, and it is being held.
His gaze is turned to the side — the wariness of one who has been hit before.
He is not on the ground — the trial has not yet finished him.

reading.upright: The Nine of Wands is resilience at the last stretch: the weariness of one who has come far, and the willingness to hold one more inch of ground.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the resilience has curdled: paranoia, exhaustion, the giving up that happens just before the end.

name: Ten of Wands
symbols: A figure carries ten wands, bent under their weight — the load is heavier than one person should carry.
The village is ahead — the destination is close, but the load has not lessened.
There is no staff — no help is being used.
His face is down — the work has taken all of the attention.

reading.upright: The Ten of Wands is the burden of responsibility carried too long: overload, fatigue, the weight that was once manageable.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the burden is being released or is collapsing: delegation, the refusal to carry what was never one's own, or the exhaustion that forces the drop.

name: Page of Wands
symbols: A youth holds a tall wand — the spark has a bearer, young and open.
A desert landscape — uncharted territory, the place before form.
A feather in the cap — flair, the pleasure of the doing.
A salamander robe — fire is his element.

reading.upright: The Page of Wands is the enthusiasm of the beginning: curiosity, the free spirit, the willingness to explore what has not been tried.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Page's fire is scattered: impatience, false starts, the boredom that comes before commitment.

name: Knight of Wands
symbols: A knight on a rearing horse — charged, ready, in motion.
A flowing plume — momentum and flair.
A desert landscape — the frontier that calls for action.
A wand held forward — the will to act, not to wait.

reading.upright: The Knight of Wands is action: bold, passionate movement toward a goal. He rides fast, and he gets there.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Knight has lost his direction: recklessness, impatience, the fire that burns out before the arrival.

name: Queen of Wands
symbols: A queen sits on a throne with wands — command, held at ease.
Sunflowers stand tall — vitality, life turned toward the sun.
A black cat at her feet — independence, a will that is not owned.
Lions carved on the throne — Leo, the sign of confident self-display.

reading.upright: The Queen of Wands is confidence: warmth, vitality, and the determination of one who is comfortable in her own fire.
reading.reversed: Reversed, her fire turns inward or outward badly: jealousy, self-doubt, the demand that others warm themselves at her flame.

name: King of Wands
symbols: A king sits with a wand upright — vision, held in place.
Salamanders on his robe — fire, the elemental of his rule.
Lions on the throne — Leo, the sign of confident leadership.
A lizard at his feet — a small creature, kept close.

reading.upright: The King of Wands is vision and leadership: the capacity to see what could be and to lead toward it. Entrepreneurship, bold strategy, natural command.
reversed: Impulsiveness, tyranny, the vision that becomes a private project at others' expense.

name: Ace of Cups
symbols: A hand from a cloud holds a chalice — the gift arrives from beyond the self.
A dove descends into the cup — peace, spirit, the messenger.
Water overflows in five streams — emotion that is being given rather than hoarded.
A pond of lotus flowers — purity, the surface where the deepest things rise.

reading.upright: The Ace of Cups is the beginning of feeling: new love, intuitive opening, the cup that overflows. It is receptivity, not pursuit.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the cup is closed or empty: emotion repressed, love refused, the intuition that has been walled off.

name: Two of Cups
symbols: Two figures face each other, cups raised — exchange, mutual regard, a meeting of equals.
A caduceus hovers between them — harmony, healing, the alignment of two wills.
A winged lion's head — passion, sanctified by the exchange.
Both cups held at the same height — the exchange is balanced.

reading.upright: The Two of Cups is the meeting of equals: partnership, mutual attraction, the felt connection between two people or two parts of the self.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the balance fails: a relationship that has become one-sided, or a connection that no longer meets.

name: Three of Cups
symbols: Three figures raise cups together — community, the shared toast.
Harvest food at their feet — abundance, gathered and shared.
Dancing posture — joy, the body's yes.
Varied dress — the group is made of distinct people, not a crowd.

reading.upright: The Three of Cups is shared joy: friendship, community, the pleasure of being together in abundance.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the community curdles: gossip, a third party interfering, or an excess that hides the isolation.

name: Four of Cups
symbols: A figure sits under a tree, arms crossed — withdrawal, and the refusal to be moved.
A fourth cup is offered from a cloud — the gift is missed by the downcast eyes.
Three cups sit at his feet — the abundance that is not being seen.
His gaze is fixed — the contemplation that has become a closed door.

reading.upright: The Four of Cups is apathy: withdrawal from what is available, contemplation that has become stuck, the offer that is not seen.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Four of Cups opens: a new awareness arrives, the cup is finally taken up, and re-engagement begins.

name: Five of Cups
symbols: A cloaked figure bows over three spilled cups — the grief is real, and it is being felt.
Two cups stand behind — what is still there, unacknowledged.
A river separates the figure from a bridge — the crossing that will come.
A dark cloak — the mourning, worn openly.

reading.upright: The Five of Cups is grief: the loss that must be felt, the regret that attends what has happened.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Five of Cups begins to move: acceptance, the two remaining cups finally seen, the turning toward the bridge.

name: Six of Cups
symbols: Two children in a courtyard — innocence, the childhood that is shared.
Six cups filled with white flowers — sweet memory, the gift of the past.
A figure walks away — leaving the courtyard, moving on.
Warm light on stone — the past, remembered kindly.

reading.upright: The Six of Cups is the sweetness of memory: nostalgia, reunion, the innocence that the past still offers.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the past has become a hiding place: an idealised memory that blocks the present, or the refusal to leave the courtyard.

name: Seven of Cups
symbols: A figure before seven floating cups — the array of options, none yet chosen.
Each cup holds something different — and some of what is shown cannot coexist.
A shadowy figure in the mist — the wish that is not what it seems.
One cup is crowned with a laurel — the one real prize among the phantoms.

reading.upright: The Seven of Cups is the field of possibility: choices, fantasy, the imagination that offers more than it can deliver.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the mist clears: a decisive choice, or the reality check that sorts the cup from the fantasy.

name: Eight of Cups
symbols: A figure walks away from eight stacked cups — the leaving is chosen, not forced.
A full moon above — the intuition that guides the departure.
A river and mountains ahead — the unknown the figure is walking toward.
The back is turned — the past is being deliberately left.

reading.upright: The Eight of Cups is the deliberate leaving: what has been built is set down, and the deeper thing is sought.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the leaving is refused: the fear that keeps one in place, or the return to what has already been left.

name: Nine of Cups
symbols: A figure sits, arms crossed, in a satisfied posture — the wish, granted.
Nine cups arc behind him — the fulfilment, gathered.
A red hat — the pleasure of the thing, worn openly.
A table cloth — the setting is at ease, not strained.

reading.upright: The Nine of Cups is contentment: the wish fulfilled, the satisfaction that can be felt in the body.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the satisfaction is hollow: a wish granted that does not satisfy, or a smugness that mistakes itself for happiness.

name: Ten of Cups
symbols: A family group with arms raised — the household, together.
A rainbow of ten cups arches above — the blessing, complete.
A house in the background — the home that holds it.
A river flows through — life continues, and it is good.

reading.upright: The Ten of Cups is the household blessing: harmony, belonging, the felt sense that one is where one should be.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the harmony is fractured: a broken home, a disconnection within the family, the ideal that has not been realised.

name: Page of Cups
symbols: A youth holds a cup, looking at it with curiosity — receptivity, the willingness to be surprised.
A fish emerges from the cup — the unexpected message, the intuition surfacing.
A sea behind — the depth from which the message comes.
Lotus flowers on the robe — purity, openness.

reading.upright: The Page of Cups is the sensitive messenger: imagination, openness to the surprising, the small intuitive signal that arrives.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the sensitivity curdles: moodiness, emotional immaturity, or the retreat into an imagined world.

name: Knight of Cups
symbols: A knight on a slow-moving horse — approach, not charge.
A cup held forward — the offering, sincere.
A river runs beside him — the feeling, moving with him.
Winged helmet — mercury, the message that is carried by feeling.

reading.upright: The Knight of Cups is the romantic approach: the offer made from the heart, charm, and the willingness to follow feeling.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the offering is unrealistic or manipulative: the charm that hides a mood, or the disappointment of a romance that was never going to arrive.

name: Queen of Cups
symbols: A queen sits by the sea — receptivity, the emotional world close at hand.
An ornate, closed cup — the feeling is contained, not spilled.
Cherubs on the throne — divine love, present in her bearing.
The sea behind her — depth, the unconscious she reads.

reading.upright: The Queen of Cups is emotional intelligence: empathy, intuition, the capacity to hold feeling without being flooded by it.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the emotional world overflows: insecurity, codependence, or a moodiness that has taken the wheel.

name: King of Cups
symbols: A king on a floating throne — calm, held even on uncertain ground.
A cup in one hand — the feeling, held with authority.
A fish leaps beside him — the unconscious, recognised but not obeyed.
The sea is choppy — the calm is chosen, not given.

reading.upright: The King of Cups is emotional mastery: composure, diplomacy, the capacity to hold feeling without being carried by it.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the mastery is a mask: manipulation by feeling, or a repression that leaks.

name: Ace of Swords
symbols: A hand from a cloud holds a sword upright — clarity, given.
A crown on the sword's tip — truth, with authority.
A laurel and a palm branch — victory, but the victory of sight.
Clouds around the hilt — the clarity emerges from what has been unclear.

reading.upright: The Ace of Swords is the breakthrough of clarity: a truth that cuts through, a decision that can now be made, a seeing that was not possible before.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the clarity fails: confusion, miscommunication, or a sword drawn too quickly and cutting the wrong thing.

name: Two of Swords
symbols: A blindfolded figure holds two swords crossed — the choice, avoided by not looking.
The sea behind her — emotion, present but not the deciding factor.
A crescent moon — intuition, available but not consulted.
The stance is balanced — the stalemate is stable, and that is the problem.

reading.upright: The Two of Swords is the stalemate: a difficult choice not yet made, a balance achieved by not looking.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the stalemate breaks: either the decision arrives, or the overload of information makes it impossible.

name: Three of Swords
symbols: Three swords pierce a heart — the pain is specific, and it is felt.
Rain falls in the background — sorrow, in the atmosphere.
Clouds gather — grief, moving through.
There is no figure — the pain is universal, not one person's alone.

reading.upright: The Three of Swords is the specific pain of knowing: heartbreak, grief, the truth that hurts because it is true.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the healing has begun: forgiveness, the release of a pain that has been held long enough.

name: Four of Swords
symbols: A figure lies on a tomb-like bed — rest, but a rest with a sword beside it.
Three swords on the wall, one beneath the bed — the conflict is suspended, not finished.
A stained-glass window — the quiet is beautiful, and it is a chosen enclosure.
The figure's hands are folded — the body has agreed to stop.

reading.upright: The Four of Swords is deliberate rest: the recuperation that must be taken, the retreat that restores.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the rest is refused or has ended: restlessness, burnout, or a return to action before the body has recovered.

name: Five of Swords
symbols: A figure gathers swords, smiling — the win, but the smile is not reassuring.
Two figures retreat in the distance — the cost, borne by the losers.
Clouds gather — the atmosphere is the aftermath, not the contest.
The winner is alone — the victory has emptied the field.

reading.upright: The Five of Swords is the conflict that has become a win at any cost: victory that leaves no ground to stand on.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the fight is being left: reconciliation, the willingness to stop, or the recognition that the win was not worth it.

name: Six of Swords
symbols: A figure sits in a boat, face turned forward — passage, underway.
A ferryman poles them across — help is being given.
Six swords stand upright in the boat — the past is being carried, not left behind.
A far shore ahead — the destination is known, though not yet arrived at.

reading.upright: The Six of Swords is the passage: movement from one shore to another, the carrying of what must be carried, the leaving of what must be left.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the boat has stalled or turned: stuck on the water, unresolved baggage dragged back, or the return to what was being left.

name: Seven of Swords
symbols: A figure sneaks away carrying five swords — the strategy, and its cost.
Two swords remain behind — the taking is partial.
A camp in the distance — the deceived, unaware.
The figure looks back — the fear of being caught.

reading.upright: The Seven of Swords is strategy at the edge of deceit: the clever move, the thing taken quietly, the self that must be watched.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the deception surfaces: coming clean, being caught, or the self-deception that can no longer be maintained.

name: Eight of Swords
symbols: A bound, blindfolded figure among eight swords — the trap is largely of the mind.
The bindings are loose — they could be slipped, if it were known.
A castle on a hill — the isolation the figure has accepted.
Wet ground — emotion, underfoot.

reading.upright: The Eight of Swords is restriction: the sense of being trapped, often by a bind that is looser than it feels.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the bindings are seen: freedom, the exit that was always there, the loosening of the self-made trap.

name: Nine of Swords
symbols: A figure sits up in bed, face in hands — the sleep that has been taken.
Nine swords hang on the wall — the thoughts that will not stop.
A dark room — the isolation of the night-mind.
The blanket is pulled close — comfort is being sought, and not found.

reading.upright: The Nine of Swords is the mind at night: anxiety, worry, the thoughts that grow larger in the dark.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the night begins to end: relief arriving, the fear released, the dawn that makes the swords smaller.

name: Ten of Swords
symbols: A figure lies face down, ten swords in the back — the end, total.
Dawn is breaking on the horizon — the ending is also a beginning.
A red cloak — the vitality that was, now spilled.
Still water beyond — the calm that follows the storm.

reading.upright: The Ten of Swords is the ending that has come: rock bottom, the finality that is also a clearing.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the recovery has begun: the worst is past, the body gets up, and the dawn that was visible is finally reached.

name: Page of Swords
symbols: A youth holds a sword, alert — the mind, awake.
Wind-blown clouds — thought, in movement.
Birds overhead — messages, small and quick.
A raised stance — readiness to engage.

reading.upright: The Page of Swords is the alert mind: curiosity, the search for truth, and the willingness to ask the difficult question.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the mind turns sharp or scattered: gossip, a truth used as a weapon, or thought that will not settle.

name: Knight of Swords
symbols: A knight charges on a rearing horse — speed, with a destination.
A sword raised — the will to use it.
Wind and clouds — the atmosphere of motion.
No saddle — the charge is direct, almost unmediated.

reading.upright: The Knight of Swords is the charge: swift action, mental drive, the willingness to cut through.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the charge has no direction: aggression, recklessness, or the burnout that follows haste.

name: Queen of Swords
symbols: A queen sits with a sword upright — reason, at rest but ready.
Clouds behind her — the thought that has gathered.
Birds in flight — perspective, the view from above.
An outstretched hand — invitation, but on her terms.

reading.upright: The Queen of Swords is clear sight: independence, boundaries, and the direct speech that respects both self and other.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the clarity has hardened: coldness, bitterness, or a cutting that no longer serves.

name: King of Swords
symbols: A king on a throne holds a sword upright — intellect, with authority.
Butterflies on the throne — transformation, understood and led.
Clouds behind — thought, gathered and settled.
An unsmiling face — judgment that does not soften itself.

reading.upright: The King of Swords is the mind in authority: judgment, ethics, the willingness to decide on principle.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the authority is misused: tyranny, coldness, or the law applied without wisdom.

name: Ace of Pentacles
symbols: A hand from a cloud holds a coin — the opportunity, given.
A garden below — the ground where the seed will fall.
An arch of foliage — a passage, a way through.
Mountains in the distance — the goal the seed will eventually reach.

reading.upright: The Ace of Pentacles is the material beginning: the offer, the seed, the opportunity that can be taken up.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the opportunity is missed or refused: the seed unplanted, or the scarcity that will not risk the ground.

name: Two of Pentacles
symbols: A figure juggles two coins within an infinity loop — the balance is active, not static.
Ships ride high waves behind — the world is moving, and the juggling is in response.
One foot lifted — readiness, the constant adjustment of the stance.
A tall hat — the performance, worn lightly.

reading.upright: The Two of Pentacles is active balance: juggling the demands, adjusting as things move, staying light on the feet.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the juggle fails: overextension, the dropped ball, or the disorganisation that the balance was hiding.

name: Three of Pentacles
symbols: A mason works on a cathedral arch — skill applied to something larger than the worker.
A monk and a nobleman consult — collaboration across different stations.
Plans held in hand — design, thought before the making.
Three coins carved into the arch — the work itself is the reward.

reading.upright: The Three of Pentacles is craft in collaboration: skilled work, joined with others, making something that none could make alone.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the collaboration falters: teamwork issues, unrecognised skill, or work that has been done without the plan.

name: Four of Pentacles
symbols: A figure holds a coin to the chest — the thing being protected.
One coin on the crown, two under the feet — holding on, in every direction.
A city behind — the security the hoard is meant to buy.
The posture is closed — the body is the vault.

reading.upright: The Four of Pentacles is holding on: security, saving, the willingness to keep what has been earned.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the holding becomes either greed or release: the grip that will not open, or the letting go that frees the hand.

name: Five of Pentacles
symbols: Two figures in the snow — hardship, endured.
A lit stained-glass window above them — help is available, but not seen.
One figure on crutches — the body is bearing the cost.
Five coins in the window — the resource that is there, behind the glass.

reading.upright: The Five of Pentacles is material hardship: loss, exclusion, the cold that has to be walked through.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the hardship begins to lift: help arrives, the door opens, and the return to warmth begins.

name: Six of Pentacles
symbols: A merchant holds scales in one hand and gives coins with the other — giving, with fairness.
Two figures kneel to receive — the receivers, in a posture of need.
The scales are balanced — the giving is not arbitrary.
A rich robe on the giver — the source of the giving is secure.

reading.upright: The Six of Pentacles is fair exchange: generosity, charity, the flow of resource from where it is to where it is needed.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the exchange is unequal: strings attached, debt, or the giving that is a way of holding power.

name: Seven of Pentacles
symbols: A figure leans on a hoe, looking at a vine — the waiting, and the assessment of the wait.
Seven coins among the leaves — the investment, growing.
The vine is heavy — the growth is real.
The figure is not harvesting yet — the timing is not yet.

reading.upright: The Seven of Pentacles is patient investment: the long growth, the willingness to wait, the assessment of what has been planted.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the waiting has become frustration: the impatience that uproots the vine, or the recognition that this investment will not return.

name: Eight of Pentacles
symbols: A figure at a workbench, carving a coin — the work, repeated and refined.
Coins already finished hang beside him — the evidence of practice.
A town behind — the world that the craft will enter.
The posture is absorbed — the attention has been given.

reading.upright: The Eight of Pentacles is the practice: the repeated work that builds mastery, the craft that is earned rather than given.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the practice is distorted: perfectionism that will not finish, drudgery that has lost its meaning, or the laziness that will not begin.

name: Nine of Pentacles
symbols: A figure stands in a garden, at ease — the abundance, earned and enjoyed.
A bird on her gloved hand — the trained instinct, a wild thing now familiar.
A rich robe — the wealth is worn, not hidden.
Nine coins among the vines — the fruit, fully grown.

reading.upright: The Nine of Pentacles is self-sufficiency: the independence that has been earned, and the pleasure of enjoying what one has built.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the independence is hollow: overwork, a dependence disguised as freedom, or the abundance that cannot be enjoyed.

name: Ten of Pentacles
symbols: An old figure seated, with a family around — the lineage, gathered.
Ten coins arranged in the Tree of Life pattern — wealth, structured.
An arch — the passage between the generations.
Dogs at the old man's feet — loyalty, kept close.

reading.upright: The Ten of Pentacles is legacy: the wealth that outlives the one who built it, the family that carries it forward.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the legacy is broken: financial loss, a family divided, or the short-term that cannot become a future.

name: Page of Pentacles
symbols: A youth holds a coin, looking at it — the opportunity, examined.
A field behind — the ground where the study will be applied.
Mountains in the distance — the goal, still far.
A focused gaze — the willingness to begin at the beginning.

reading.upright: The Page of Pentacles is the beginning of practical learning: the student, the apprentice, the willingness to start small and to study.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the study is unfocused or refused: the opportunity missed, the laziness that will not begin, or the plan that is not a plan.

name: Knight of Pentacles
symbols: A knight on a still, dark horse — the pace is slow, and it is deliberate.
A coin held in the hand — the responsibility, taken seriously.
Fields behind — the ground being worked.
The horse is not rearing — the motion is steady, not dramatic.

reading.upright: The Knight of Pentacles is the slow, reliable worker: diligence, responsibility, the progress that is measured in years rather than days.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the steady has become stuck: stagnation, the laziness that calls itself caution, or the stubborn refusal to move.

name: Queen of Pentacles
symbols: A queen sits in a garden — practicality, growing things, the world tended.
A coin held in her lap — the resource, kept close.
Rabbits nearby — fertility, the multiplication of what is cared for.
A rich robe and a canopy of leaves — abundance, made habitable.

reading.upright: The Queen of Pentacles is practical nurture: the resourcefulness that makes a home, the abundance that is shared, the ground that holds others.
reversed: Reversed, the nurture is distorted: neglect, smothering, or the overwork that empties the one who tends the ground.

name: King of Pentacles
symbols: A king sits on a throne in a garden — rule, held with ease.
A coin in one hand and a scepter in the other — wealth and authority, together.
Vines climb around him — abundance, growing where he is.
A bull's head on the throne — Taurus, the sign of endurance.

reading.upright: The King of Pentacles is the secure ruler of the material world: prosperity, stability, the leadership that comes from having built something real.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the security is hardened: greed, stubbornness, or the materialism that cannot see past its own ground.
